lesson.title: Why Computers Never Get Bored: An Introduction to Loops
lesson.summary: Loops let a program repeat a block of instructions without the programmer writing that block out over and over, turning tedious repetition into a few lines of reusable code.
lesson.body:
Imagine you needed a program to print "Happy Birthday" one hundred times. Without a special tool for repetition, you would have to type the same print statement one hundred separate times, and if you later needed one hundred and fifty, you would have to go back and add fifty more lines by hand. That is exactly the kind of problem loops solve. A loop is a control structure that repeats a block of code, either a fixed number of times or until some condition changes, so you write the instructions once and let the computer execute them again and again on its own.

Loops belong to the same family as the branching statements you already know from control flow. An if statement changes which path execution takes through your code, choosing one branch and skipping the others, but it still only runs each chosen line a single time. A loop changes execution in a different way: it sends the program's instruction pointer backward, to the top of a block, instead of forward past it, which is what allows the same lines to run again. Both are departures from the default behavior of running statements once, top to bottom, and both give you real power over what actually happens when the program runs, rather than locking you into a single straight-line script.

Every loop needs two things to make sense: something to repeat, and a way to know when to stop. Python gives you two loop forms that answer that "when to stop" question differently. A for loop repeats once for each item in a sequence, so it naturally stops when the sequence runs out of items. A while loop repeats as long as a boolean condition stays true, so it stops the moment that condition becomes false. Both forms are covered in detail in their own sections, but it helps to see one in action first, since the idea is easiest to understand through a concrete trace.

Consider this short loop:
for count in range(1, 4):
    print(count, "Mississippi")
Trace it step by step. The first time through, count is 1, so the program prints "1 Mississippi". The second time, count is 2, printing "2 Mississippi". The third time, count is 3, printing "3 Mississippi". After that, range(1, 4) has no more values to offer, so the loop stops and the program moves on to whatever comes after it. Three lines get printed from two lines of code, and the exact same pattern would work whether you needed 3 repetitions or 3,000, with no extra typing required.

This matters far beyond birthday messages and counting games. Real programs use loops to process every row in a spreadsheet, every pixel in an image, every character in a password the user typed, or every enemy on screen in a video game. Almost any task that can be phrased as "do this for each..." or "keep doing this until..." is a signal that a loop belongs in your solution, and learning to recognize that signal quickly is one of the most useful instincts you can build as a programmer, long before you master every detail of the syntax itself.
